title: Learning to Be Guided: Shaping Latent Geometry for Classifier-Free Guidance

paper.title: Learning to Be Guided: Shaping Latent Geometry for Classifier-Free Guidance
paper.abstract:
Abstract † † footnotetext: ∗ Equal contribution. Correspondence to: {haoming.liu, hongyi.wen}@nyu.edu . Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard component of conditional diffusion models, and guided generation performance has become the de facto measure of state-of-the-art models.
Recent work on latent diffusion models seeks to learn latent spaces that are easier to model with diffusion.
However, under CFG, generation additionally depends on how conditions are arranged in the latent space.
We study this arrangement under discrete class conditions, termed class geometry , and investigate what class geometry allows a latent space to work well with CFG.
Under a Gaussian class model, we show that shifting variance from intra- to inter-class at fixed total variance makes classes more distinguishable under noise, and derive a noisy posterior objective whose per-sample descent direction is proportional to the oracle CFG correction.
Based on the analysis, we propose Prototype Regularization (PR), a lightweight surrogate for the intractable noisy posterior objective, which applies a cosine prototype classifier to spatially pooled latents.
With a controlled training budget (20 epochs for VAE, 80 epochs for DiT), adding PR to an LDM baseline reduces guided gFID on ImageNet from 3.31 to 2.28, surpassing a DINOv3-aligned VA-VAE (2.44) with negligible overhead.
We further demonstrate that PR generalizes to pseudo-labels derived from clustering, continuous text-embedding conditions, and video latents.
Together, our findings highlight class geometry as a critical factor in guided generation and take a first step toward CFG-compatible representation learning.
Our project page is available at: https://maps-research.github.io/cfg-geometry/ .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) have become a predominant paradigm in generative modeling, with recent advances largely driven by conditional generation on auxiliary signals such as class labels and text ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . Classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) is a standard technique for strengthening the conditioning: during sampling, a single model makes conditional and unconditional predictions, and their displacement (i.e., the CFG correction) is amplified by a guidance scale ω > 1 \omega>1 . CFG improves generation quality and has become a crucial component of state-of-the-art models: headline results are generally reported under CFG, usually with a large margin over unguided sampling. Consequently, guided performance has become the de facto measure of a conditional diffusion model. In parallel, latent diffusion models (LDMs) ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) have become the prevailing approach for generating high-dimensional data: an autoencoder first compresses data into a compact latent space, and a diffusion model is then trained in this latent space. A growing line of research designs latent spaces that are easier to model, either by aligning latents with pretrained representations ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Leng et al., 2025 ) or by adopting pretrained representations directly as the latent space ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) , while another line of analysis studies which properties of a latent space make it easier for diffusion models to learn ( Skorokhodov et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . These efforts primarily approach latent design through the lens of diffusability , i.e., how easily a diffusion model learns the latent distribution. Under CFG, however, the guided score for a condition c c takes the form ∇ z t ​ log ​ p t ​ ( z t ) + ω ​ ∇ z t ​ log ​ p t ​ ( c ∣ z t )

More precisely, since p t ​ ( c ∣ z t ) p_{t}(c\mid z_{t}) is evaluated on noisy latents, what matters is how distinguishable this arrangement remains under noise corruption. To characterize this arrangement more explicitly, we ground our analysis in discrete class conditions, where it reduces to the layout of classes, termed class geometry . We thus ask: what class geometry allows a latent space to work well with CFG? We address this question by analyzing the CFG correction term through the lens of class geometry (Sec. 2 ). Specifically, under a Gaussian class model, we derive the oracle CFG correction in closed form: it contrasts the target class mean against competing class means, weighted by their noisy posteriors. We then show that, at fixed total variance, reallocating variance from intra-class to inter-class makes classes more distinguishable under noise, so the target class posterior concentrates earlier in denoising. Finally, we express this geometric preference as a cross-entropy objective on the noisy class posterior, whose per-sample descent direction is proportional to the oracle correction. Guided by our analysis, we propose Prototype Regularization (PR), a tractable surrogate for the posterior objective on clean latents (Sec. 3 ). In practice, PR applies a cosine prototype classifier to spatially pooled latents, and we show that its gradient forms a target-versus-competitor contrast analogous to that in the oracle CFG correction. On ImageNet class-conditional generation, adding PR to an LDM baseline reduces guided gFID from 3.31 to 2.28, outperforming DINOv3-aligned ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) VA-VAE (2.44) ( Yao et al., 2025 ) with negligible overhead (Sec. 4.2 ). To isolate the source of this gain, we transplant PR class centers into LDM latents and recover most of PR’s guided improvement, indicating that the gain stems largely from class geometry (Sec. 4.3 ). We further demonstrate the versatility of PR through extensions to pseudo-labels, video latents, and continuous text conditions (Sec. 4.4 , 4.5 , 4.6 ). Since PR relies only on discrete partitions to promote a cluster geometry, these results suggest that it applies beyond ground-truth labels whenever this geometry stays informative under noise. Together, our work highlights class geometry as a critical factor in guided generation and takes a first step toward CFG-compatible representation learning. Our contributions are threefold: • We analyze CFG through the lens of class geometry. Under a Gaussian class model, we derive the closed-form oracle correction, show that shifting variance from intra- to inter-class at fixed total variance improves class distinguishability under noise, and formulate a noisy posterior objective whose per-sample descent direction is proportional to this correction. • We propose Prototype Regularization (PR), a lightweight surrogate for the noisy posterior objective that shapes class geometry. By classifying clean latents against prototypes, PR yields gradients analogous to the target-versus-competitor contrast in the oracle correction. • We show that PR generalizes across label sources, modalities, and condition types, suggesting its effectiveness as a CFG-compatible geometry regularizer over discrete partitions.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Our primary testbed is class-conditional image generation on ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution. We build on the VA-VAE codebase ( Yao et al., 2025 ) and use a convolution-based encoder/decoder with a latent shape of 32 × 16 × 16 32\times 16\times 16 , paired with LightningDiT-XL/1 as the stage-2 backbone. We use the same number of training epochs for all methods (20 epochs for stage-1 and 80 epochs for stage-2) for fair comparison. All ImageNet experiments in the main text are trained on 8 × 8\times NVIDIA H100 GPUs; a subset of appendix experiments uses 2 GPUs (with 10 epochs for stage-1 and 30 epochs for stage-2). Full hyper-parameter details are provided in Appendix C . We use generation FID (gFID) ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) as our primary metric, which measures how closely generated images match the training distribution. For all results with classifier-free guidance, we report gFID at the best guidance scale ω ⋆ \omega^{\star} , selected via a guidance scale sweep using gFID computed on 5K samples. When comparing against baselines, we follow the standard practice and additionally report sFID, Inception Score (IS), Precision, and Recall using the ADM evaluation toolkit ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) . All metrics are computed over 50K samples unless otherwise stated. Setups for Sec. 4.5 and Sec. 4.6 are described in their respective subsections.

sections.heading: 4.2 Class-Conditional Image Generation with Ground-truth Labels
sections.text: We compare PR against LDM ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) and VA-VAE ( Yao et al., 2025 ) . We trained two VA-VAE variants, aligned with DINOv3-B and DINOv3-L ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) , respectively. Our method integrates PR into LDM training. On reconstruction fidelity, we report PSNR, LPIPS, and rFID. Overall, all methods perform comparably, with VA-VAE holding a marginal edge. PR therefore does not sacrifice reconstruction quality for class geometry. Meanwhile, PR raises Purity@10 (i.e., the fraction of each latent’s 10 nearest neighbors that share its class) from 0.020 0.020 (LDM) to 0.279 0.279 , about 4 × 4\times that of the strongest VA-VAE variant ( 0.071 0.071 ), indicating substantially more class-consistent local neighborhoods. PR achieves this at negligible cost, whereas VA-VAE slows stage-1 training throughput by about 25 % 25\% due to the additional representation alignment. On the generation side, the gains of PR concentrate on guided settings. Without CFG, PR improves over LDM ( 13.09 → 11.59 13.09\rightarrow 11.59 ) but trails both VA-VAE variants. With CFG, PR takes the lead, achieving the best gFID ( 2.28 2.28 ), IS ( 269.85 269.85 ), and Recall ( 0.585 0.585 ) among all methods. Moreover, the gFID ranking with CFG is consistent with the Purity ranking, while the ranking without CFG differs. This suggests that class geometry is particularly relevant to guided generation quality, which we investigate further in Section 4.3 . Both VA-VAE and PR exhibit lower Precision and higher Recall than LDM under CFG, suggesting broader coverage of the data distribution at a cost in sample fidelity. Figure 2 examines the latent spaces from three complementary angles: (a) We decompose the energy of per-channel normalized latents into a global mean, inter-class variation, and intra-class variation. In LDM, over 90 % 90\% of the energy belongs to the intra-class portion. VA-VAE mildly increases inter-class energy, but shifts a large portion to the global mean, a spatial template shared by all latents. PR reallocates intra-class energy to inter-class variance, yielding the largest inter-class share among all methods. PR yields substantially higher target-class posteriors across a broad range of noise levels, demonstrating improved class distinguishability under noise. sections.heading: 4.3 Understanding the Gains through Center Transplantation
sections.text: Figure 2 (a) shows that PR primarily reallocates latent energy to inter-class variance (i.e., more separated class centers). This raises a natural question: can an unregularized latent space benefit from the class geometry of PR in a plug-and-play manner? To answer this, we transplant reference class centers into the LDM latent space. For a latent z z of class c c , we replace its native center with a reference center, z ′ = z − μ c LDM + μ c Ref z^{\prime}=z-\mu_{c}^{\mathrm{LDM}}+\mu_{c}^{\mathrm{Ref}} , which preserves intra-class deviations, and train a stage-2 model on z ′ z^{\prime} . To ensure the decoder receives latents in its native space, we apply the inverse mapping before decoding. We use two PR references: the full center and its spatially pooled version. As controls, we use LDM’s own centers rescaled to match the inter-class energy of the full PR centers, and random directions with PR’s per-class norms. As presented in Tab. 2 , transplanting PR centers improves guided generation (gFID 3.31 → 2.52 3.31\rightarrow 2.52 with pooled centers), while the unguided setting changes only marginally ( 13.09 → 12.65 13.09\rightarrow 12.65 ). Increasing the inter-class energy of LDM alone yields a partial gain ( 2.89 2.89 ), and PR centers improve further beyond this energy-matched control. In contrast, random directions provide little benefit with CFG and even hurt unguided generation. These results indicate that PR centers have a better arrangement, and the gain does not stem from increased inter-class energy alone. Besides, pooled centers outperform spatially resolved ones ( 2.52 2.52 vs. 2.63 2.63 ), so the useful class signal is mainly a global channel-wise offset. Interestingly, transplanting PR or random centers shifts ω ⋆ \omega^{\star} upward (3.5 to 4.5), whereas rescaling LDM’s own centers does not (2.0). However, a larger ω ⋆ \omega^{\star} does not by itself imply better geometry: random centers admit the strongest guidance yet bring little gain in guided quality, while rescaled LDM centers improve quality without changing ω ⋆ \omega^{\star} . Hence, the optimal guidance scale and the quality attained at it should be considered separately. Finally, center transplantation recovers most of PR’s guided gain but only a small portion of its unguided gain, and thus does not fully reproduce the benefits of PR. This is likely because transplantation only alters inter-class separation and leaves intra-class spread untouched, whereas PR reshapes both during stage-1 training.

sections.text: Building on PR’s performance gains on ground-truth class labels, we further investigate whether PR remains effective on other types of labels, and whether the two stages must share the same label set. To this end, we construct unsupervised labels by clustering the [CLS] tokens of DINOv3-L ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) with spherical K K -means, setting K = 1000 K{=}1000 to match the number of ImageNet classes. We then evaluate all combinations of stage-1 PR labels and stage-2 conditioning labels (Tab. 3 ). When conditioning on DINO clusters, we sample cluster labels in proportion to cluster sizes during evaluation. sections.heading: 4.5 Generalization to Video Latents
sections.text: We further examine whether PR generalizes to video latents. We conduct experiments on UCF-101 ( Soomro et al., 2012 ) , a human action video dataset spanning 101 action classes, and adopt LeanVAE-16 ( Cheng and Yuan, 2025 ) as the base autoencoder. This VAE is trained with reconstruction objectives and compresses each 17-frame 256 × 256 256\times 256 clip into a latent of shape 5 × 16 × 32 × 32 5\times 16\times 32\times 32 ( T × C × H × W T\times C\times H\times W ). Starting from the official VAE checkpoint, we fine-tune for 3 epochs using either reconstruction alone or reconstruction with PR; for video latents, PR’s average pooling spans both the spatial and temporal dimensions. We then fine-tune a Latte-XL/2 model ( Ma et al., 2025 ) on each of three latent spaces: the official VAE, the VAE fine-tuned with reconstruction alone, and the VAE fine-tuned with PR. All three Stage 2 runs are initialized from the EMA weights of the same Latte-XL/2 checkpoint provided by LeanVAE and fine-tuned for 50K steps with a global batch size of 10. We also evaluate the VAE and Latte-XL/2 checkpoints provided by LeanVAE without further training as a reference. We report FVD (over 2048 clips), which measures the distance between the generated and real video distributions, and action classification accuracy from a pre-trained UCF-101 classifier, which measures the class consistency of conditional generation. As shown in Tab. 4 , PR improves FVD in both settings with on-par accuracy, reducing FVD from 152.7 152.7 to 140.1 140.1 with CFG and from 287.3 287.3 to 275.7 275.7 without CFG. These results suggest that the benefit of PR is not specific to images and extends to latent spaces of other modalities. sections.heading: 4.6 Generalization to Continuous Conditioning
sections.text: Finally, we examine whether PR benefits generation under continuous conditioning signals. We consider text-to-image generation on ImageNet: we caption each image with Florence-2-large ( Xiao et al., 2024 ) and encode the caption into a CLIP ViT-L/14 text embedding ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , which replaces the class embedding in LightningDiT ( Yao et al., 2025 ) through a small MLP adapter. Besides LDM and VA-VAE (DINOv3-L), we compare against two continuous alignment baselines, which align latents via cosine similarity to pre-trained features projected to the channel dimension by PCA. We apply 1000-class PR with ground-truth classes, clusters of CLIP-L text embeddings, and DINOv3-L [CLS] tokens. All metrics are computed on 50K images generated from held-out validation captions. As shown in Tab. 5 , PR variants lead on all three metrics under guidance, with cluster labels consistently outperforming cosine alignment to the same representation. Meanwhile, clusters of CLIP-L text or DINOv3-L image embeddings yield performance comparable to ground-truth classes. Without CFG, VA-VAE performs best, consistent with its leading gFID in Tab. 1 . Since captions typically group around shared objects or scenes, the latent geometry induced by PR may help organize representations along semantic groupings reflected in the captions, making it informative for text-conditioned generation. Together, these results demonstrate that PR improves guided text-to-image generation without requiring ground-truth class labels.

sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Latent Representation for Diffusion Models. Latent diffusion models (LDMs) adopt a two-stage paradigm ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) : an autoencoder maps high-dimensional data to a compact latent space, and a diffusion model learns to generate within it. Subsequent work expands the design space by widening the latent channels ( Esser et al., 2024 ; Labs et al., 2025 ) and raising the compression ratio ( Chen et al., 2025e ) . Recent work focuses on improving latent representations. One line of work uses pretrained representations as supervision: VA-VAE ( Yao et al., 2025 ) aligns latents with pretrained features during autoencoder training; REPA-E ( Leng et al., 2025 ) enables end-to-end tuning through REPA alignment ( Yu et al., 2024 ) ; MAETok ( Chen et al., 2025b ) uses masked modeling with auxiliary decoders. Another line builds on pretrained encoders: AlignTok ( Chen et al., 2025a ) adapts a pretrained encoder through multi-stage training; RAE ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Singh et al., 2026 ) uses frozen pretrained representations as diffusion latents; and SVG ( Shi et al., 2026 ) augments frozen DINO features with learned residual features. VTP ( Yao et al., 2026 ) further explores joint training objectives, combining image-text contrastive, self-supervised, and reconstruction losses. Diffusability of Latent Representations. Recent work studies latent diffusability (i.e., how easily diffusion models learn a latent distribution). Some approaches focus on spectral structure and spatial equivariance: Skorokhodov et al. (2025) use scale-equivariance regularization to suppress excessive high-frequency content; EQ-VAE ( Kouzelis et al., 2025 ) promotes equivariance by matching reconstructions of transformed latents to transformed images; SSVAE ( Liu et al., 2026 ) studies latent spectral properties in video. Others regularize the latent distribution directly: UL ( Heek et al., 2026 ) uses a learned diffusion prior; DMVAE ( Ye et al., 2025 ) aligns the aggregate latent distribution with a reference via score-based distribution matching. Complementary studies examine multiple properties jointly: PAE ( Yue et al., 2026 ) highlights spatial structure, local manifold continuity, and global semantics; Zhong et al. (2026) identify velocity irreducible variance, semantic separability, and spatial structure as consistent predictors of generation quality in a large-scale study. Classifier-Free Guidance. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) strengthens conditioning at inference at the cost of reduced diversity, with subsequent works refining this trade-off in sampling ( Karras et al., 2024 ; Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) . Analyses show that CFG does not sample from the intended tilted distribution ( Bradley and Nakkiran, 2024 ; Chidambaram et al., 2024 ) and raises classification confidence while reducing diversity ( Wu et al., 2024 ) . It can be decomposed into a class-mean shift and contrastive components in linear models ( Li et al., 2025 ) , or viewed as pushing trajectories away from decision boundaries ( Zhao and Schwing, 2026 ) . Pavasovic et al. (2025) show that in high dimensions CFG acts mainly during class selection, consistent with the vanishing correction in Fig. 1 (a). These works primarily analyze CFG under a given data distribution; we instead treat the latent space as a design variable and study which class geometry facilitates CFG. Class Separation for Guided Generation. Recent work links CFG to class separation: Ventura et al. (2026) show that CFG distorts the conditional target when classes are poorly separated. MCLR ( Li et al., 2026 ) attributes the reliance on CFG to weak separation between learned conditionals and enlarges it by maximizing inter-class likelihood ratios when training the generator; more broadly, guidance-free training internalizes the effect of CFG into the generator ( Chen et al., 2025c ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025d ) . ProtoDiffusion ( Baykal et al., 2024 ) instead modifies the conditioning, replacing learned class embeddings with pretrained class prototypes. These methods change how the generator is trained or conditioned while keeping the data representation fixed, whereas PR reshapes the latent space itself to promote class separation in the diffusion target.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: Unguided performance. PR primarily targets guided generation, where its gains concentrate; without guidance, it still improves over LDM but trails VA-VAE (Tab. 1 ). The remaining gap may stem from average pooling, which constrains only the channel dimension and leaves spatial structure unregularized, while suppressing high-frequency spatial components has been shown to be helpful for diffusability ( Skorokhodov et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Since PR leaves the spatial residual unconstrained, it can be combined with regularizers that shape other aspects of the latent space: applying PR on top of VA-VAE improves both guided and unguided generation (Appendix D.5 ). Scope of analysis. Under Gaussian forward corruption, Tweedie’s formula links the posterior gradient to the Bayes-optimal CFG correction (Eq. 6 ) without assuming Gaussian latents (Appendix E.7 ). The Gaussian class model additionally provides a closed-form correction and predicts how variance reallocation affects noisy class separation and posterior uncertainty. The empirical posterior trend is consistent with these predictions (Fig. 2 (b)). Appendix F further discusses how class geometry relates to other CFG quantities, complementing the posterior-based analysis. Design space of PR. PR instantiates the posterior objective through two design choices, the time distribution ρ \rho and the approximation of q c q_{c} , both of which leave room for exploration (Appendix D.1 ). For ρ \rho , clean-latent supervision avoids the over-regularization of noisy supervision, though intermediate distributions may offer better trade-offs. For q c q_{c} , the pooled prototype classifier is one of many ways to realize the target-versus-competitor contrast.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we study CFG-compatible representation learning through the lens of class geometry. Our analysis links the oracle CFG correction to how distinguishable classes remain under noise, which motivates Prototype Regularization (PR), a lightweight regularizer that shapes class geometry and improves guided generation. PR generalizes across label choices, data modalities, and condition signals, suggesting that aligning latent geometry through categorical priors is a simple yet effective way to design latent spaces for guided generation. Given that CFG is used almost universally at sampling time, we hope this work encourages treating CFG compatibility as an explicit and principled axis of latent design, alongside reconstruction and generation quality.

sections.text: Velocity irreducible variance has been studied as a statistical indicator of latent diffusability ( Zhong et al., 2026 ) . Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard component of conditional diffusion models, and guided generation performance has become the de facto measure of state-of-the-art models. Recent work on latent diffusion models seeks to learn latent spaces that are easier to model with diffusion. However, under CFG, generation additionally depends on how conditions are arranged in the latent space. We study this arrangement under discrete class conditions, termed class geometry , and investigate what class geometry allows a latent space to work well with CFG. Under a Gaussian class model, we show that shifting variance from intra- to inter-class at fixed total variance makes classes more distinguishable under noise, and derive a noisy posterior objective whose per-sample descent direction is proportional to the oracle CFG correction. Based on the analysis, we propose Prototype Regularization (PR), a lightweight surrogate for the intractable noisy posterior objective, which applies a cosine prototype classifier to spatially pooled latents. With a controlled training budget (20 epochs for VAE, 80 epochs for DiT), adding PR to an LDM baseline reduces guided gFID on ImageNet from 3.31 to 2.28, surpassing a DINOv3-aligned VA-VAE (2.44) with negligible overhead. We further demonstrate that PR generalizes to pseudo-labels derived from clustering, continuous text-embedding conditions, and video latents. Together, our findings highlight class geometry as a critical factor in guided generation and take a first step toward CFG-compatible representation learning. Our project page is available at: https://maps-research.github.io/cfg-geometry/ . 1 Introduction Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) have become a predominant paradigm in generative modeling, with recent advances largely driven by conditional generation on auxiliary signals such as class labels and text ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . Classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) is a standard technique for strengthening the conditioning: during sampling, a single model makes conditional and unconditional predictions, and their displacement (i.e., the CFG correction) is amplified by a guidance scale ω > 1 \omega>1 . CFG improves generation quality and has become a crucial component of state-of-the-art models: headline results are generally reported under CFG, usually with a large margin over unguided sampling. Consequently, guided performance has become the de facto measure of a conditional diffusion model. In parallel, latent diffusion models (LDMs) ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) have become the prevailing approach for generating high-dimensional data: an autoencoder first compresses data into a compact latent space, and a diffusion model is then trained in this latent space. A growing line of research designs latent spaces that are easier to model, either by aligning latents with pretrained representations ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Leng et al., 2025 ) or by adopting pretrained representations directly as the latent space ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) , while another line of analysis studies which properties of a latent space make it easier for diffusion models to learn ( Skorokhodov et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . These efforts primarily approach latent design through the lens of diffusability , i.e., how easily a diffusion model learns the latent distribution. Under CFG, however, the guided score for a condition c c takes the form ∇ z t ​ log ​ p t ​ ( z t ) + ω ​ ∇ z t ​ log ​ p t ​ ( c ∣ z t )

More precisely, since p t ​ ( c ∣ z t ) p_{t}(c\mid z_{t}) is evaluated on noisy latents, what matters is how distinguishable this arrangement remains under noise corruption. To characterize this arrangement more explicitly, we ground our analysis in discrete class conditions, where it reduces to the layout of classes, termed class geometry . We thus ask: what class geometry allows a latent space to work well with CFG? We address this question by analyzing the CFG correction term through the lens of class geometry (Sec. 2 ). Specifically, under a Gaussian class model, we derive the oracle CFG correction in closed form: it contrasts the target class mean against competing class means, weighted by their noisy posteriors. We then show that, at fixed total variance, reallocating variance from intra-class to inter-class makes classes more distinguishable under noise, so the target class posterior concentrates earlier in denoising. Finally, we express this geometric preference as a cross-entropy objective on the noisy class posterior, whose per-sample descent direction is proportional to the oracle correction. Guided by our analysis, we propose Prototype Regularization (PR), a tractable surrogate for the posterior objective on clean latents (Sec. 3 ). In practice, PR applies a cosine prototype classifier to spatially pooled latents, and we show that its gradient forms a target-versus-competitor contrast analogous to that in the oracle CFG correction. On ImageNet class-conditional generation, adding PR to an LDM baseline reduces guided gFID from 3.31 to 2.28, outperforming DINOv3-aligned ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) VA-VAE (2.44) ( Yao et al., 2025 ) with negligible overhead (Sec. 4.2 ). To isolate the source of this gain, we transplant PR class centers into LDM latents and recover most of PR’s guided improvement, indicating that the gain stems largely from class geometry (Sec. 4.3 ). We further demonstrate the versatility of PR through extensions to pseudo-labels, video latents, and continuous text conditions (Sec. 4.4 , 4.5 , 4.6 ). Since PR relies only on discrete partitions to promote a cluster geometry, these results suggest that it applies beyond ground-truth labels whenever this geometry stays informative under noise. Together, our work highlights class geometry as a critical factor in guided generation and takes a first step toward CFG-compatible representation learning. Our contributions are threefold: • We analyze CFG through the lens of class geometry. Under a Gaussian class model, we derive the closed-form oracle correction, show that shifting variance from intra- to inter-class at fixed total variance improves class distinguishability under noise, and formulate a noisy posterior objective whose per-sample descent direction is proportional to this correction. • We propose Prototype Regularization (PR), a lightweight surrogate for the noisy posterior objective that shapes class geometry.
